0: If you’re a fund manager setting up an ESG (environmental, social and governance, the criteria investors use to rate companies) policy, failing to consider Bitcoin in the mix amounts to gross negligence on your ESG obligations.
2: If you’re a private investor, not investing in Bitcoin because it “uses energy” is like not investing in solar panels because they “use energy” (coal in solar’s case) in their manufacture. That is a 101-level cost-accounting error. It fails to look at both cost and benefit to establish a net ESG position.
4: Reading the latest [[0|IPCC]] and [[1|UNEP]] reports made us realize something. We, and by extension any ESG fund, have an urgent duty to look at technologies that can have a faster impact on climate change.
7: We are especially impressed that Bitcoin has reached 58.4% [[2|sustainable energy]] use. This is not only [[3|higher than any other industry sector]]. It is also a higher share of total energy use than any [[4|large industrialized country]] achieves.
8: It has achieved this in just 14 years. Our research found a [[5|renewable growth rate of 59%]] since Q1 2021, and ~383% from 2013. This matters because it can be a “[[6|Roger Bannister]]” to other industries, by showing that a seemingly impossible speed is in fact possible.
9: Bitcoin mining’s renewable adoption story can show other progressive industries what’s possible. It also removes the excuse from laggard industries that a rapid move to renewables is impossible.
10: More important, from an ESG cost-accounting view, we are interested in the net environmental benefits of Bitcoin mining. That means looking at how Bitcoin mining can speed up measures to reduce climate change.
17: We also looked for evidence that the ESG case for Bitcoin can grow exponentially. We again found plenty. A year ago, there was 1 Bitcoin mining company helping remove flared methane gas. At the time of writing there are 10 (7 removing methane in oil&gas), 1 removing methane from [[9|landfills]], and 2 using biogas).
19: We found that [[10|no technology other than Bitcoin mining]] could [[11|economically use flared gas]]. Other uses would require building high-voltage pylons @ $2M/mile, or gas pipelines @ $5M+/mile. Further, in some places where governments regulated flaring, venting rose: a far worse climate problem.
20: This is a quick summary of a 2-month DD (due diligence process). We realize that not everyone has time for that level of DD. That is why we’re happy to share our models and research with other funds, fund managers and private investors who want to make sensible ESG decisions about Bitcoin.
3: First some background. I’m a fund manager for an ESG fund. I’ve been investing in new technologies since 2000. Our tech investment funds have focused on deep-tech solutions that remove carbon from industrial processes. The impact of those technologies will be felt from 2035 onwards.
18: Above all, we asked ourselves whether other technologies or processes could do the job that Bitcoin does. For example, could flared methane be used for other goods? Could flaring (burning off unwanted natural gas at oil wells, which still releases unburned methane) be reduced by better regulation?
